note_claims.claim: The patient presents with a dry cough lasting approximately 2 months.
The patient has a persistent dry, tickly, non-productive cough.
The patient denies haemoptysis, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, breathlessness, chest pain, heartburn, voice change, or dysphagia.
The patient has a history of ramipril use for hypertension, increasing the dose from 2.5 mg to 5 mg in July.
The cough began after the patient started ramipril.
The patient is an ex-smoker who quit 20 years ago, having previously smoked about 10 cigarettes a day for approximately 15 years (7.5 pack-years).
The patient has a known history of asthma.
The patient is currently taking ramipril 10 mg once daily and atorvastatin 20 mg at night.
The chest examination is clear bilaterally, and the throat is normal.
The persistent dry cough is most likely induced by an ACE inhibitor.
The plan is to stop ramipril and switch the patient to losartan 50 mg once daily.
A blood test for U&Es and salt levels is planned one to two weeks after starting losartan.
A chest X-ray is ordered due to the patient's history of being an ex-smoker and having a cough for 2 months.
The patient is advised that the cough may take up to 3 months to resolve after stopping ramipril.
The patient is advised to contact the practice sooner if they experience haemoptysis, breathlessness, unintentional weight loss, or chest pain.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician greeted Mr Penhaligon and asked if he had brought someone with him.
Patient stated his wife, Margaret, does the remembering.
Relative stated someone has to remember.
Patient reports a dry, tickly cough that never stops.
Patient states the cough has been going on for about six weeks.
Relative stated the cough started before the patient's sister's birthday, early August.
Patient corrected the timing, stating it was more like two months.
Clinician asked if the patient brings anything up when coughing.
Patient stated nothing is brought up, and the cough is completely dry.
Clinician asked about blood.
Patient stated no blood.
Clinician asked about fevers, night sweats, or weight loss.
Patient stated no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss, but mentioned putting on a bit of weight.
Clinician asked about breathlessness or chest pain.
Patient stated no breathlessness or chest pain, and that he is fine walking the dog.
Clinician asked about heartburn or acid coming up into the throat.
Patient stated no heartburn.
Clinician asked about change in voice or trouble swallowing.
Patient stated no change in voice or trouble swallowing.
Clinician asked about smoking history.
Patient stated he gave up smoking 20 years ago, but previously smoked about ten a day for maybe fifteen years.
Clinician referenced the record showing ramipril was started in the summer, June.
Patient stated ramipril was started at the end of May.
Relative recalled ramipril started at the end of May because they had just returned from Whitby.
Patient confirmed the start date was the end of May.
Clinician asked about the current dose.
Patient stated the current dose is five milligrams once a day, and that the dose was increased from 2.5 mg in July.
Clinician thanked the patient and asked about other medicines.
Patient stated he is also taking atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night.
Clinician asked about allergies to medicines.
Patient stated he has no known drug allergies.
Relative stated she coughs at night, but her cough is due to asthma, and advised not to put it in his notes.
Clinician asked if the patient had ever had asthma.
Patient stated he has never had asthma.
Clinician examined the chest and throat, finding them clear, and measured the blood pressure as 134 over 82.
Patient stated the blood pressure was better than before.
Clinician suggested ramipril might be causing the cough, noting it is a well-known side effect and the timing fits (cough started after starting ramipril).
Patient expressed surprise, stating he thought he might have picked something up.
Clinician suggested stopping ramipril and switching to losartan 50 mg once daily, which works similarly but doesn't usually cause a cough.
Patient asked what the dose of losartan would be.
Clinician stated they would start losartan at 50 milligrams once a day.
Clinician requested a blood test to check kidneys and salt levels one to two weeks after starting losartan.
Clinician stated they would see the patient again in four weeks to check blood pressure.
Relative asked if the cough would go straight away.
Clinician stated the cough may take a few weeks, sometimes up to three months, to settle after stopping ramipril.
Patient acknowledged this information.
Clinician suggested arranging a chest X-ray to be thorough, given the patient's history of being an ex-smoker and having a cough for a couple of months.
Patient agreed to the chest X-ray.
Clinician instructed the patient to contact them sooner if they cough up any blood, become short of breath, lose weight without trying, or get any chest pain.
Patient acknowledged the safety instructions.
Relative stated she would keep an eye on him.
Clinician stated that if the cough hasn't improved at all by the four-week review, they will think again about other causes.
Patient thanked the doctor.
